title: Introduction to Meet in the Middle
description: Halve an exponential search by solving two halves and combining them cleverly

blocks.text: Meet in the middle is a powerful technique for problems that look hopelessly exponential. When brute force would examine 2 to the power n possibilities, this method examines only about 2 to the power n over 2, which is the square root of the original work.

The idea is beautifully simple: split the input into two halves, solve each half completely on its own, and then combine the two partial answers cleverly. The combination step is where all the magic happens.

blocks.caption: Split the items into two halves, enumerate each, then combine the results
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406654608-454773222.png

By the end of this topic you will know exactly when to reach for meet in the middle, how to implement it, why it is so much faster, and the common traps to avoid. It is a technique that feels like a superpower the first time it turns an impossible problem into an easy one.

content.title: 1. The Core Idea and Why Brute Force Fails

blocks.text: Many hard problems ask you to search over all subsets of a set, or all ways to pick items. The number of subsets of n items is 2 to the power n, which grows explosively. At n equals 40, that is over a trillion, far beyond what we can enumerate.
Meet in the middle attacks this by cutting the set into two halves of size n over 2 each. Each half has only 2 to the power n over 2 subsets, a number we absolutely can enumerate.

We generate every partial result for the left half and every partial result for the right half separately. Then we ask: which left result pairs with which right result to form a full solution? Answering that quickly is the whole trick.

items: Full brute force scans 2 to the power n possibilities
Split the input into two halves of n over 2 items each
Each half has only 2 to the power n over 2 possibilities
Combine one half against the other to build full solutions

blocks.text:
The name explained:

You work inward from both ends of the problem and the two halves "meet in the middle" during the combine step. Neither half alone is a solution; the answer lives in how they join.
Consider the classic subset sum problem: given a set of numbers, is there a subset that adds up to a target value? The obvious solution tries every subset.

blocks.caption: At n equals 40, brute force must examine over a trillion subsets
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406654609-222347305.png
blocks.alt: The Core Idea and Why Brute Force Fails

blocks.text: With n items there are 2 to the power n subsets. For each we compute a sum and check it against the target. Here is that brute force, which is fine for small n but collapses beyond about n equals 25.
This is O(2^n). At n equals 40 it would run for far too long. Yet n equals 40 is exactly the kind of constraint where meet in the middle shines.
The first move is to divide the items into two groups, a left half and a right half, each with about n over 2 elements. Which items go where does not matter, only that the split is even.

blocks.caption: Splitting the items turns 2^n work into two piles of 2^(n/2) work
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406654609-229955132.png
For the subset sum problem, we now enumerate every possible subset sum of the left half, and separately every possible subset sum of the right half. Each list has 2 to the power n over 2 entries.

At n equals 40, each half has 20 items, so each list has about a million entries. A million is trivial to generate and store, whereas a trillion was not. This single split is what makes the problem tractable.
Now comes the clever part. A full subset is one piece from the left plus one piece from the right. So a full subset sum equals some left sum plus some right sum.

blocks.caption: For each left sum, binary search the right half for the exact complement
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406654609-297946847.png

We want a total equal to the target. So for each sum s taken from the left list, we need a sum equal to target minus s in the right list. If we can find that complement quickly, we have found a valid full subset.

To search the right list quickly, we sort it once, then use binary search for each complement. Sorting costs about 2 to the power n over 2 times its logarithm, and each of the 2 to the power n over 2 lookups is logarithmic. The whole combine step stays close to 2 to the power n over 2.

The combine step is the heart:

Generating the halves is easy. The art is combining them fast. Sorting one half and binary searching, or using a hash set, is what keeps the whole method near the square root of the brute force cost.
Let us trace a small case. Take the set 3, 34, 4, 12 and a target of 16.

blocks.caption: Split the set, list each half sums, then match a left sum with its complement on the right
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406654610-302532343.png
Split into left equal to 3, 34 and right equal to 4, 12. The left subset sums are 0, 3, 34, and 37. The right subset sums are 0, 4, 12, and 16.

Now scan the left sums. For 0 we need 16 on the right, and 16 is present, so the answer is yes. The matching subset is the empty set from the left plus 4 and 12 from the right, which indeed sums to 16. We found it without ever listing all 16 subsets of the full set.

items: Left sums: 0, 3, 34, 37
Right sums (sorted): 0, 4, 12, 16
For left sum 0, the needed complement is 16, which exists
The subset is 4 and 12, confirming the target is reachable

content.title: 5. Meet in the Middle in Code

blocks.text: Here is the full solution. We build the subset sums of each half, sort the right half, then binary search each complement.

Note that some languages let us skip sorting by using a hash set for the right half, which makes each lookup constant time. Sorting with binary search is the version to know when you also need ordered queries, like closest sum.

content.title: 6. Why It Is So Much Faster

blocks.text: The whole point is the exponent. Brute force is 2 to the power n. Meet in the middle is roughly 2 to the power n over 2, multiplied by a small logarithmic factor for the search.

blocks.caption: The exponent halves, so a trillion operations become a few million
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406654610-171261092.png
blocks.alt: Why It Is So Much Faster

blocks.text: Halving the exponent is an enormous win, because it is the same as taking a square root of the total work. A trillion becomes a million. Something that would run for years finishes in a blink.

items: Brute force: O(2^n) time
Meet in the middle: O(2^(n/2) times n) time
Space: O(2^(n/2)) to store the half you search
The exponent is halved, which square roots the running time

blocks.text: The speed does not come for free. To search one half quickly, we must store all of its 2 to the power n over 2 partial results. That is the memory price of the technique.

At n equals 40 that is about a million values, which is comfortable. But push n much higher and the storage itself becomes the bottleneck. This is why meet in the middle has a sweet spot rather than being universal.

Time buys space:

Meet in the middle trades memory for speed. You store one half so you can query it fast. Always check that the stored half fits in memory before committing to the approach.
Often you need more than a yes or no answer; you need the actual subset that hits the target. Meet in the middle supports this with a small addition.

Instead of storing only the sums for each half, store the sum together with the bitmask that produced it. When a left sum matches a right complement, you combine their two masks to recover exactly which items were chosen.

codes.python:
# store (sum, mask) for one half so we can rebuild the chosen items
def subset_sums_with_mask(a):
    n = len(a)
    out = []
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        s = sum(a[i] for i in range(n) if mask & (1 << i))
        out.append((s, mask))       # keep the mask alongside the sum
    return out

blocks.text: The left mask tells you which of the left items were picked, and the right mask tells you which right items were picked. Together they name the full subset that reaches the target.
The subset sum check is just the starting point. The same split and combine pattern solves many related problems.

items: Count subsets that reach a target, by counting matches instead of stopping at the first
Closest subset sum to a target, by binary searching for the nearest value in the sorted half
Subset sum within a range, by counting right sums in an interval with two binary searches
Four number sum, splitting four arrays into two pairs and matching their sums

blocks.text: The four number sum variation is a favourite. You compute all pairwise sums of the first two arrays, store them in a map, then for every pairwise sum of the last two arrays you look up the needed complement.

blocks.caption: The four sum problem splits into two pairs whose sums are matched through a map
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406654610-402152658.png

A frequent twist asks not for an exact target, but for the subset sum that is closest to a target without exceeding it, or closest in absolute value. Meet in the middle handles this with a tiny change to the combine step.

Instead of a binary search for an exact complement, we binary search the sorted half for the value nearest to what we need. The candidate just below and just above the ideal complement are both checked.

codes.python:
import bisect
def closest_sum(a, target):
    n = len(a)
    A = subset_sums(a[: n // 2])
    B = sorted(subset_sums(a[n // 2 :]))
    best = 0
    for s in A:
        need = target - s                       # ideal right value
        j = bisect.bisect_right(B, need)         # first value above need
        if j > 0:
            cand = s + B[j - 1]                  # the value at or below need
            if abs(target - cand) < abs(target - best):
                best = cand
    return best

blocks.text: This is why we often prefer the sorted half with binary search over a plain hash set. Ordered data lets us answer nearest and range questions, not just exact matches.

content.title: 9. Meet in the Middle vs Dynamic Programming

blocks.text: Subset sum also has a well known dynamic programming solution, so why bother with meet in the middle? The answer is about the size of the numbers, not the count of them.

The DP for subset sum runs in time proportional to n times the target value. That is wonderful when the target is small, say a few thousand, but it becomes impossible when the values and target are huge, like up to 10 to the power 18.

Meet in the middle does not care how large the values are. Its cost depends only on n, the number of items. So the two techniques cover different regimes, and knowing which to pick is part of the skill.

items: Dynamic programming: fast when the target value is small, but scales with that value
Meet in the middle: fast when n is around 40, no matter how large the values are
Huge values plus small n is the signal to abandon DP and split instead
Small values plus large n is the signal to use DP

blocks.text:
Read the constraints:

If the numbers are gigantic but there are only about 40 of them, dynamic programming is out and meet in the middle is almost certainly the intended solution.

content.title: 10. When and Where to Use It

blocks.text: The clearest signal is the constraint on n. Meet in the middle lives in a very specific band.

items: The problem is naturally exponential, over subsets or choices
n is too large for full brute force, roughly above 25
n is small enough that n over 2 is enumerable, roughly up to 40 or 45
Partial answers from two halves can be combined by matching values

blocks.text: That n around 40 constraint is almost a fingerprint. When you see it on an otherwise exponential problem, meet in the middle should be the first idea you try.
Meet in the middle is a recurring guest in contests and interviews, almost always with that medium sized n.

items: Subset sum and partition problems where values are enormous
Choosing items to hit or approach a budget, like the closest subset sum
Four number sum and its relatives across split arrays
Puzzle style search problems with around 40 binary choices

blocks.text: If you train your eye to spot the exponential shape paired with an n near 40, you will recognise these instantly and reach for the split without hesitation.
A few mistakes trip people up when implementing this technique.

items: Overflow: subset sums can be large, so use a 64 bit integer type
Forgetting the empty subset: a sum of zero is a valid partial result and must be included
Uneven split: splitting badly wastes the benefit, so keep the halves close to equal
Slow combine: if you scan the second half linearly instead of sorting or hashing, you are back to quadratic in the halves

blocks.text:
The combine step decides everything:

If the merge is not fast, the whole technique loses its advantage. Always sort with binary search or use a hash structure so each match is logarithmic or constant.
When you suspect this technique fits, work through these steps.

items: Confirm the problem is exponential and that n is around 30 to 45
Decide what a partial answer for half the items looks like, usually a sum
Split the items into two even halves
Enumerate every partial answer for each half
Sort or hash one half so it can be queried fast
For each partial answer in the other half, look up the complement you need

blocks.text: Follow this and even a scary looking exponential problem becomes a routine two step exercise: enumerate the halves, then match them.
If you remember one picture, make it this: a problem too big to cross in one leap, split down the middle, with both sides walking toward each other until they meet.
Neither half is the answer. The answer is the handshake in the middle, where a partial result from the left meets exactly the partial result it needs from the right.
Whenever you see an exponential problem with a medium n, picture that handshake. It is the fastest way to recall both what the technique does and why it works.
Meet in the middle is one of those techniques that changes what feels possible.

items: It halves the exponent, turning O(2^n) into about O(2^(n/2))
Split the input, solve both halves, then combine by matching values
The combine step, powered by sorting and binary search or hashing, is the key
It costs extra memory to store one half, so watch the space
The n around 40 constraint is the classic hint that it applies

blocks.text: Whenever an exponential problem has that tell tale medium sized n, remember that you can meet in the middle and take a square root off the running time.
